sittings.bodyEn: After a long summit, his father saw a photo of the highest-paying clients and thought the room was too big to be a premium group. Those people were the Gym Lords, each paying $42,000 a year. The father asked whether the price was even legal, and whether the clients knew what they were paying. The reply was a trade: if the work added $239,000 to the year, would $42,000 be worth it. The owner's effort was about 15 hours a week, the extra revenue showed up over 11 months, and nothing was due before the system started making the money. Once those terms were clear, the price made sense, and this chapter is about building that kind of gap on purpose.

terms.hook: The buyer pays a high price because the result is worth more than the check.

sittings.bodyEn: People buy when they believe the value is worth more than the price. When value falls below the price, they stop buying, and he calls that gap the price to value discrepancy. A sketch in the chapter shows value starting above a flat price line and later crossing a point of cancellation. He uses a plain distinction: price is what you pay, and value is what you get. The fastest way to widen the gap is a lower price, and that move usually shrinks the business because the aim is profit. Price can fall only to zero, so unless your costs are about a tenth of a rival's, raise the value first and then the price, as in $100,000 of value for $10,000.

terms.hook: Value must stay above price, or the buyer reaches a point of cancellation.
The moment perceived value drops under the price and they stop buying.

sittings.bodyEn: A pricing teacher he follows puts it this way: being second cheapest has no strategic benefit, and being the most expensive does. Most owners still look at the market, take the average, and slip a little under it. They add a little extra and land on more for less. The rivals they copy are often broke, because that average is the price of an efficient market. More competitors keep offering a little more for a little less until the margin only stays above water, the weakest operators wash out, and new owners repeat the loop. The goal here is the most money, and a premium price is what funds a level of help the average price cannot carry.

terms.hook: The price left after everyone copies a little more for a little less, with barely any margin.
A price high enough to fund exceptional delivery and a real profit.

sittings.bodyEn: He draws a vicious cycle beside a virtuous one, with a column for the client and a column for the business. Drop the price and the client invests less emotion, perceives less value, and gets weaker results. They also become more demanding, and you have less revenue per customer to fulfill the promise. On the business side, profit falls, you think less of the work, you see less impact, service levels drop, and the sales team believes it less. The service then gets worse because there is too little money left to make it exceptional. He lived that squeeze, and he asks owners who care about clients and staff to fund the work at a price that can actually deliver.

terms.hook: A lower price weakens investment, results, service, profit, and the team's belief.

sittings.bodyEn: Raise the price and those same rows flip in the other direction. Clients invest more, perceive more value, get better results, demand less, and leave you more money to fulfill each one. Profit rises, you respect the work more, you see more impact, service rises, and the sales team speaks with more conviction. That margin pays for systems, strong people, a better experience, and a longer runway to help more people. The people who pay more also pay more attention, so a price that stings a little focuses them on using what they bought. When they follow through and get better results, the higher price has created more value in practice.

terms.hook: A higher price raises investment, results, service, profit, and conviction together.

sittings.bodyEn: In a study, people rated a cheap wine, a mid-priced wine, and an expensive wine while the prices were visible. They ranked the glasses in price order. All three glasses were the same wine. A higher price can raise the value people experience with no other change to the product. The aim is a price far enough above the pack that the buyer assumes something different is going on. In that frame you sit in a category of one, and you can earn profit that comes from having no real comparison.

terms.hook: People can taste the same wine as better when the price they see is higher.

sittings.bodyEn: If the customer must take action to get the result, they need to be invested in the outcome. A price that stings a little creates that investment and pulls their attention onto the work. Charging the fee still requires the product to deliver what was promised. He says the nerve to ask comes from doing the work so many times that self-doubt loses. Experience is what lets you request a large share of someone's year and still stand behind it. The belief has to remain when you are alone with it, because a shortcut on delivery fails once real clients arrive.

terms.hook: A fee that stings enough to make the buyer take the work seriously.

sittings.bodyEn: Before the offer was a product, he flew to 33 gyms in 18 months, fixed the operation, and relaunched it in 21 days. Those relaunches averaged $42,000 in extra sales across the 21 days, and his fee was all of that new revenue. Eight turnarounds a month turned the travel into a string of motels. One month he tried to cancel, the owner insisted on help, and he agreed to teach the process while the owner did the work. That gym collected almost $44,000 in new upfront sales within 30 days, about four times the prior month. The process could be taught from a distance, and they later reached more than 4,000 gyms with a done-with-you model.

terms.hook: The client does the work from a process you have already proved in person.

sittings.bodyEn: When he entered, low-priced rivals sold full-service marketing for $500 a month, and one high-priced rival charged $5,000. He wanted the premium slot, expensive enough that the price itself created allure. The offer was $16,000 for a 16-week done-with-you intensive, about three times the expensive rival and about 32 times the cheap one. About 35 percent of those buyers then moved into a three-year agreement at $42,000 a year. The average gym owner took home $35,280 a year, so many were committing half a year of pay or more. He could ask for that amount, young and unknown to them, because his conviction was stronger than their doubt.

terms.hook: A price well above the current high option, so the offer feels like its own category.

sittings.bodyEn: A voluntary survey of 158 gyms that had been in the program for 11 months matched the conviction he already had. Top-line revenue rose about $19,932 a month, about $239,000 a year, and recurring revenue rose about $13,339 a month. Monthly profit moved from $2,943 to $8,940, a bit more than triple, and the client count rose by 67. The share of clients leaving each month fell from just under 11 percent to just under 7 percent, retail rose $4,400 a month, and prices moved from $129 to $167. Clients still received a deal, because they paid a fraction of the extra revenue and the gap between price and value stayed wide. He says 99 percent of businesses need to raise prices to grow, because profit is the oxygen that lets you reach more people, and a free lesson on this gap sits with the chapter.

terms.hook: Margin is what lets you make bets, serve better, and reach more people.

sittings.bodyEn: The virtuous cycle claims that price changes the buyer's behavior and the firm's ability to deliver. The vicious cycle is the same chart with the arrows reversed. Second cheapest is called out as a position with no strategic benefit. Choose what a higher price does in this chapter.
sittings.prompt: What does a higher price do in the virtuous cycle?
choices: It raises the client's investment, perceived value, and follow-through, and it funds better delivery
It lowers investment because the buyer feels punished and quits
It helps only when you are the second cheapest option in the market
It leaves results unchanged because price is only a label on the same work
